newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Novartis reports strong sales in quarter.
newsitem.headline: Novartis reports strong sales in quarter.

text.p: Novartis AG said Thursday that first-quarter sales rose 22 percent and growth was particularly strong in pharmaceuticals, thanks to a good performance in the United States.

The Swiss pharmaceuticals and life sciences group -- which was formed at the start of the year through the merger Ciba-Geigy AG and Sandoz AG -- said sales rose to 8.18 billion Swiss francs ($5.6 billion) from 6.68 billion ($4.54 billion) in 1996.
Sales in pharmaceuticals, its largest single business segment, totalled 3.39 billion ($2.31 billion), representing an increase of 30 percent in Swiss francs and 14 percent in local currencies.
"The sales growth of 14 percent in the pharmaceuticals sector was driven by the performance in the United States, where sales in the previous year were comparably low," Novartis said in a statement.
Novartis also reiterated its optimistism about its prospects for 1997, but said growth was not likely to remain at these relatively lofty levels for the rest of the year.

"We are very confident about the entire year, that means we see strong growth rates. But I have to say that I would not expect that we would see exceptionally high figures throughout the year," Chief Financial Officer Raymund Breu said in a telephone interview.
Group sales for the period were 8 percent higher when computed in local currencies. Novartis said the 22 percent Swiss franc sales increase was due to the strong positive currency effect.
The Swiss franc has weakened substantially against most other major currencies since early 1996.
The group's agribusiness sales were 17 percent higher, or 4 percent higher on a local currency basis. Nutrition division sales rose by 18 percent in Swiss francs and by 3 percent in local currencies.
Novartis reported increases in Swiss franc terms in all divisional categories except animal health, where sales declined by 8 percent in Swiss francs and by 22 percent on a local currency basis.

Breu said the decline was due to an inventory reduction process at the distributor level taking place in the United States since last year. High inventories were being reduced in the group's Programme dog flea control product, he said.
Consumer demand for the product had not declined, but factory sales were down as a result of the inventory reduction, Breu said.
The company said that it had restated 1996 figures for comparison purposes and, accordingly, the prior-year figures do not include divested business activities.
The biggest divestiture was the spin-off last month of Ciba Speciality Chemicals, a company that accounted for some 6.7 billion francs ($4.6 billion) in sales during 1996.
